The coefficient of $t^k$ is $E[X^k]/k!$, so the $k$-th derivative at $t=0$ peels off exactly $E[X^k]$. The MGF is a power series whose coefficients *are* the moments, differentiation is just reading off the term you want. A caution the exam occasionally tests: an MGF does not always exist. It requires $E[e^{tX}]$ to be finite on an interval around $0$, which fails for heavy-tailed laws like the lognormal or Cauchy, their tails grow faster than $e^{tx}$ can be tamed. When an MGF exists, though, it is unique, so two variables sharing an MGF share everything.

sections.title: The three properties you will actually use
sections.body: **Moments:** $E[X^k] = M^{(k)}(0)$. So $E[X] = M'(0)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = M''(0) - [M'(0)]^2$. **Uniqueness:** if two variables have the same MGF on an interval around 0, they have the same distribution, match the MGF to a known form to identify it. **Independent sums:** if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, $M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t)\,M_Y(t)$; and $M_{aX+b}(t) = e^{bt}M_X(at)$.

sections.title: More canonical MGFs, and the linear-transform rule
sections.body: Add these to your recognition set: **Binomial$(n,p)$**: $\big(1-p+pe^t\big)^n$. **Geometric$(p)$** (trials form): $\dfrac{pe^t}{1-(1-p)e^t}$. **Bernoulli$(p)$**: $1-p+pe^t$. The **linear transform** rides the constant outside and the scale inside the argument: $$M_{aX+b}(t)=e^{bt}M_X(at).$$ So scaling stretches the $t$-axis and shifting tacks on an exponential factor, it does *not* multiply $M_X$ by $a$.

sections.title: Reading moments off an MGF
sections.body: A random variable has $M(t) = (1 - 250t)^{-4}$ for $t < 1/250$. Find its mean and variance.
steps: (This is a Gamma with shape 4, scale 250: mean $= 4\cdot250 = 1000$, variance $= 4\cdot250^2 = 250\,000$, the MGF identified it.)

sections.title: Turning a sum of independents into a product
sections.body: $X \sim \text{Normal}(2, 9)$ and $Y \sim \text{Normal}(1, 16)$ are independent. Use MGFs to find the distribution of $X + Y$.
steps: Write each MGF from the normal form $e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}$: $M_X(t) = e^{2t + 9t^2/2}$ and $M_Y(t) = e^{t + 16t^2/2}$.
Independence means the sum's MGF is the *product*: $M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t)\,M_Y(t) = e^{(2+1)t + (9+16)t^2/2} = e^{3t + 25t^2/2}$.
Pattern-match the result back to $e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}$: $\mu = 3$, $\sigma^2 = 25$. By uniqueness, $X+Y \sim \text{Normal}(3, 25)$.
Cross-check: for independent variables means add ($2+1=3$) and variances add ($9+16=25$). The MGF does more, it *proves the sum is still normal*, not merely that the first two moments add. ✓

sections.title: Identify the distribution from its MGF
sections.body: A variable has MGF $M(t)=\big(0.3 + 0.7e^t\big)^5$. Name the distribution and give its mean and variance, without differentiating.
steps: Pattern-match to the binomial MGF $\big(1-p+pe^t\big)^n$: here $1-p=0.3$ and $p=0.7$ with $n=5$.
So $X\sim\text{Binomial}(5,\,0.7)$ by the uniqueness property, the MGF fingerprints it.
Quote the moments from memory: mean $=np = 5(0.7)=3.5$; variance $=np(1-p)=5(0.7)(0.3)=1.05$.

sections.title: Match the form, skip the calculus
sections.body: Memorize the canonical MGFs and you often never differentiate. Poisson$(\lambda)$: $e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}$. Normal$(\mu,\sigma^2)$: $e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}$. Gamma$(\alpha,\theta)$: $(1-\theta t)^{-\alpha}$. Exponential$(\lambda)$ is Gamma with $\alpha=1$: $(1-t/\lambda)^{-1} = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda-t}$. When an MGF appears, try to read off its parameters by pattern-matching, then quote the mean and variance from memory.

sections.title: Subtract the square, and respect the $e^{bt}$ shift
sections.body: $M''(0)$ gives $E[X^2]$, **not** the variance, you still subtract $[M'(0)]^2$. Forgetting this is the single most common MGF error. Second trap: for a linear transform $aX+b$, the MGF is $e^{bt}M_X(at)$, with the constant riding *outside* as $e^{bt}$ and the scale going *inside* the argument, do not multiply $M_X$ by $a$.

sections.title: The MGF need not exist, and mind its interval
sections.body: Two slips: (1) assuming every variable has an MGF, heavy-tailed distributions (lognormal, Cauchy, some Paretos) have $E[e^{tX}]=\infty$ for all $t>0$, so no MGF exists and you must use other tools. (2) Quoting an MGF without its domain, forms like $(1-\theta t)^{-\alpha}$ only hold for $t<1/\theta$; evaluating outside that interval is meaningless even though the derivatives at $0$ are fine.

cards.front: Why does the $k$-th derivative of $M(t)$ at $0$ produce $E[X^k]$, and why must you still subtract for variance?
cards.back: Expanding $M(t)=E[e^{tX}] = 1 + tE[X] + \frac{t^2}{2!}E[X^2] + \cdots$ makes the coefficient of $t^k$ equal $E[X^k]/k!$, so differentiating $k$ times and setting $t=0$ isolates $E[X^k]$. But $M''(0)=E[X^2]$ is the *raw* second moment, so variance still needs $M''(0) - [M'(0)]^2$, forgetting that subtraction is the classic MGF error.

cards.front: Why does an independent sum multiply MGFs, and what does the uniqueness property buy you?
cards.back: $M_{X+Y}(t)=E[e^{t(X+Y)}]=E[e^{tX}e^{tY}]$, and independence factors the expectation into $M_X(t)M_Y(t)$. Uniqueness says an MGF fingerprints exactly one distribution, so after multiplying you can pattern-match the product to a known form and *identify* the sum's distribution, proving, e.g., that independent normals sum to a normal, not just that their moments add.

cards.front: How do you read off Binomial vs Poisson vs Normal directly from an MGF?
cards.back: Binomial$(n,p)$: $(1-p+pe^t)^n$ (a power of a Bernoulli MGF). Poisson$(\lambda)$: $e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}$ (double exponential in $t$). Normal$(\mu,\sigma^2)$: $e^{\mu t+\sigma^2 t^2/2}$ (exponential of a quadratic). Match the algebraic *shape* to read parameters, then quote moments, uniqueness guarantees the match is the distribution.

cards.front: Why might a distribution have no MGF, and why does it matter?
cards.back: The MGF $E[e^{tX}]$ must be finite on an interval around $t=0$. Heavy-tailed laws (lognormal, Cauchy) have tails that overwhelm $e^{tx}$, so the integral diverges for every $t>0$ and no MGF exists. It matters because the MGF tricks, moment extraction, summing independents, identification, then simply do not apply; you fall back on the CDF or characteristic function.

questions.q: $M(t) = e^{3t + 8t^2}$. What are the mean and variance of $X$?
questions.explain: Match $e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}$: $\mu = 3$ and $\sigma^2/2 = 8 \Rightarrow \sigma^2 = 16$.

questions.q: $X$ has MGF $M(t) = \frac{1}{1-2t}$ for $t < 1/2$. Find $E[X^2]$.
$X$ and $Y$ are independent with $M_X(t) = e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}$ and $M_Y(t) = e^{\mu(e^t-1)}$. The distribution of $X+Y$ is:
questions.explain: Product of MGFs: $e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}e^{\mu(e^t-1)} = e^{(\lambda+\mu)(e^t-1)}$, Poisson$(\lambda+\mu)$.

questions.q: If $M_X(t) = (1-3t)^{-2}$, find the MGF of $Y = 2X + 1$.
$M(t) = 0.3 + 0.7e^t$. Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.
A random variable has moment generating function $M(t) = (0.3e^t + 0.7)^5$. Calculate $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.
questions.explain: Match the form $(pe^t + (1-p))^n$: this is Binomial$(n=5, p=0.3)$. So $\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p) = 5(0.3)(0.7) = 1.05$. Answer 1.50 is the mean $np$; 0.30 is just $p$.

questions.q: $X$ has moment generating function $M_X(t) = e^{2t + 3t^2}$. Calculate $\mathrm{Var}(2X - 1)$.
questions.explain: Match the normal MGF $e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}$: here $\mu = 2$ and $\sigma^2/2 = 3 \Rightarrow \sigma^2 = 6$. The shift $-1$ drops out and the scale enters squared: $\mathrm{Var}(2X-1) = 4(6) = 24$. Reading $\sigma^2 = 3$ (forgetting the $/2$) gives 12.

concepts.title: Transformations of a Random Variable
concepts.tagline: Given the distribution of $X$, find the distribution of $Y=g(X)$. The CDF method always works; the Jacobian shortcut is faster when $g$ is monotone.

sections.body: The exam rarely hands you the variable you want. It gives you $X$ and asks about $Y = X^2$, or $Y = e^X$, or $Y = \sqrt{X}$. There is one method that *never* fails, go through the CDF, and one shortcut that is faster when the transform is one-to-one. Knowing which to reach for is the whole game.

sections.title: Chase the probability through the CDF
sections.body: A transformation reshapes the density, but probabilities of *events* are preserved. So translate the question about $Y$ into an equivalent question about $X$: $F_Y(y) = P(Y \le y) = P(g(X) \le y)$. Solve the inequality for $X$, evaluate using the known CDF of $X$, then differentiate to get the density of $Y$. You are simply following the same probability mass to its new location on the $y$-axis. When $g$ is monotone *decreasing*, the same Jacobian formula works but the inverse's derivative is negative, which is exactly why the formula takes the **absolute value**: a density can never be negative, and the $|\cdot|$ records the stretch while discarding the flip in direction. For a *discrete* variable there is no Jacobian at all, you just relabel the support and sum the pmf over every $x$ that maps to each new value.

sections.title: CDF method and the Jacobian shortcut
sections.body: **CDF method (always works):** $F_Y(y) = P(g(X)\le y)$; differentiate to get $f_Y(y)$. **Jacobian (monotone $g$ only):** if $y=g(x)$ is one-to-one with inverse $x = g^{-1}(y)$, then $f_Y(y) = f_X\!\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\left|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|$. The absolute value of the derivative is the **Jacobian**, it rescales the density so total area stays 1.

sections.title: A non-monotone transform: $Y = X^2$
sections.body: Let $X \sim \text{Uniform}(-1, 1)$, so $f_X(x) = \tfrac12$ on $[-1,1]$. Find the density of $Y = X^2$.
steps: $g(x)=x^2$ is **not** monotone on $[-1,1]$, so use the CDF method. For $0 \le y \le 1$: $F_Y(y) = P(X^2 \le y) = P(-\sqrt{y} \le X \le \sqrt{y})$.
$= \int_{-\sqrt{y}}^{\sqrt{y}} \tfrac12\,dx = \tfrac12\,(2\sqrt{y}) = \sqrt{y}$.
Differentiate: $f_Y(y) = \frac{d}{dy}\sqrt{y} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}$ for $0 < y < 1$.
Note the density blows up near 0 and the support collapsed to $[0,1]$, exactly why you cannot just plug into the Jacobian formula here.

sections.title: A monotone transform via the Jacobian
sections.body: Let $X \sim \text{Exponential}(1)$, so $f_X(x) = e^{-x}$ for $x > 0$. Find the density of $Y = \sqrt{X}$.
steps: Here $g(x)=\sqrt{x}$ *is* monotone increasing on $x>0$, so the Jacobian shortcut applies. Invert: $x = g^{-1}(y) = y^2$.
Jacobian (the stretch factor): $\dfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y) = \dfrac{d}{dy}y^2 = 2y$, and $|2y| = 2y$ for $y>0$.
Assemble: $f_Y(y) = f_X(y^2)\,|2y| = e^{-y^2}\cdot 2y = 2y\,e^{-y^2}$ for $y>0$ (a Rayleigh density).

Update the support and cross-check it integrates to 1: $x>0 \Rightarrow y>0$, and $\int_0^\infty 2y\,e^{-y^2}\,dy = \big[-e^{-y^2}\big]_0^\infty = 1$. ✓ The Jacobian rescaled the density so the total area is preserved.

sections.title: Inverse-CDF transform: turning a uniform into an exponential
sections.body: Let $U\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)$ and define $Y=-\tfrac{1}{\lambda}\ln(1-U)$. Show $Y$ is exponential with rate $\lambda$ (this is how simulators generate exponential draws).
steps: $g(u)=-\tfrac1\lambda\ln(1-u)$ is monotone increasing on $(0,1)$, so go through the CDF. $F_Y(y)=P(Y\le y)=P\!\big(-\tfrac1\lambda\ln(1-U)\le y\big)$.
Solve the inequality for $U$: $\ln(1-U)\ge -\lambda y \Rightarrow 1-U\ge e^{-\lambda y} \Rightarrow U\le 1-e^{-\lambda y}$.
Since $U$ is uniform, $P(U\le c)=c$ on $(0,1)$: $F_Y(y)=1-e^{-\lambda y}$ for $y>0$.
That is exactly the Exponential$(\lambda)$ CDF, so $f_Y(y)=\lambda e^{-\lambda y}$. This is the **inverse-transform method**: feeding a uniform through $F^{-1}$ produces any target distribution. ✓

sections.title: Probability integral transform
sections.body: Two universal facts the exam exploits: (1) If $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ then $X = F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$, this is how you *simulate* any distribution. (2) Going the other way, if $X$ has continuous CDF $F$, then $F(X) \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$. So a transform like $Y = 1 - e^{-\lambda X}$ applied to an exponential is *exactly* its own CDF, making $Y$ uniform on $(0,1)$ instantly, no integration needed.

sections.title: Monotonicity and the new support
sections.body: Never apply the Jacobian formula to a non-monotone $g$ (like $x^2$ over a symmetric interval), you will miss half the probability. When $g$ folds the line, split into monotone pieces or use the CDF method. Second trap: always restate the **support** of $Y$. The range of $g$ over the support of $X$ sets where $f_Y$ is nonzero; forgetting to update it produces a density that does not integrate to 1.

sections.title: Decreasing transforms still need the absolute value
sections.body: For a decreasing $g$ (say $Y=e^{-X}$), the inverse derivative $\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)$ is **negative**. Dropping the absolute value in $f_Y(y)=f_X(g^{-1}(y))\,|\,(g^{-1})'(y)\,|$ yields a negative 'density', an immediate red flag. The Jacobian measures a *stretch*, so only its magnitude enters; the sign just tells you $g$ reversed orientation.

cards.front: Why does the CDF method work for *any* transform when the Jacobian doesn't?
cards.back: Events keep their probability even after $g$ reshapes the density, so $F_Y(y)=P(g(X)\le y)$ just rewrites the question in terms of $X$, solves the inequality, and reads off the known $F_X$, then differentiate for $f_Y$. It never assumes $g$ is one-to-one, so it handles folds like $x^2$ that map two $x$'s to one $y$, where the Jacobian would silently miss half the mass.

cards.front: What does the Jacobian $|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)|$ do, and why must you restate the support of $Y$?
cards.back: For a monotone $g$ the Jacobian is the local stretch factor: it rescales $f_X$ so that probability is conserved when the axis is stretched or compressed, keeping the total area at 1. You must also map the support, the range of $g$ over $X$'s support sets where $f_Y$ is nonzero; skip that and the 'density' won't integrate to 1.

cards.front: What is the inverse-transform method, and why does $F(X)\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)$?
cards.back: If $U\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)$ then $X=F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$, so feeding a uniform through the inverse CDF generates *any* distribution, the basis of simulation. The converse holds because $P(F(X)\le u)=P(X\le F^{-1}(u))=F(F^{-1}(u))=u$, so $F(X)$ is uniform whenever $F$ is continuous. The CDF maps a variable onto its own probability scale.

cards.front: Why does the Jacobian carry an absolute value, and what replaces it for discrete variables?
cards.back: The Jacobian $|(g^{-1})'(y)|$ is a local stretch factor that conserves probability mass; a decreasing $g$ gives a negative derivative, but densities cannot be negative, so only the magnitude counts (the sign merely flips orientation). Discrete variables have no Jacobian, transforming just relabels outcomes, so you sum the pmf over every preimage $x$ with $g(x)=y$.

questions.q: $X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ and $Y = -\ln X$. The distribution of $Y$ is:
questions.explain: $F_Y(y)=P(-\ln X\le y)=P(X\ge e^{-y})=1-e^{-y}$ for $y>0$, exponential, rate 1, mean 1.

questions.q: $X$ has density $f_X(x)=2x$ on $(0,1)$. Let $Y=X^2$. Find $f_Y(y)$ on $(0,1)$.
questions.explain: $g$ is monotone. $x=\sqrt{y}$, $\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}$. $f_Y=2\sqrt{y}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}=1$, uniform on $(0,1)$.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$. The distribution of $Y=1-e^{-\lambda X}$ is:
questions.explain: $1-e^{-\lambda x}$ is the exponential CDF, so $Y=F(X)\sim$ Uniform$(0,1)$ by the probability integral transform.

questions.q: $X\sim N(0,1)$ and $Y=e^{X}$. The variable $Y$ is called:
questions.explain: By definition, the exponential of a normal is lognormal.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Uniform}(0,2)$ and $Y=3X+1$. The density $f_Y(y)$ is constant equal to:
questions.explain: Linear monotone transform: $Y$ is uniform on $(1,7)$, length 6, so $f_Y=\frac16$.

questions.q: $X$ is exponential with mean 1, so $f_X(x) = e^{-x}$ for $x>0$. Let $Y = e^{-X}$. What is the distribution of $Y$?
questions.explain: $F_Y(y) = P(e^{-X} \le y) = P(X \ge -\ln y) = e^{-(-\ln y)} = y$ for $0<y<1$. A CDF of $F_Y(y)=y$ is Uniform$(0,1)$, this is the probability integral transform ($Y = F_X(X)$ applied to an exponential's own survival form).

questions.q: $X$ is uniform on $(-2, 2)$, so $f_X(x) = \frac14$. Let $Y = X^2$. Find the density $f_Y(y)$ for $0 < y < 4$.
questions.explain: $Y=X^2$ is non-monotone, so use the CDF method: $F_Y(y) = P(-\sqrt{y} \le X \le \sqrt{y}) = \frac14(2\sqrt{y}) = \frac{\sqrt{y}}{2}$. Differentiate: $f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}$. Treating it as monotone (one branch) drops the factor of 2 and gives $\frac{1}{8\sqrt{y}}$.

concepts.title: Percentiles, Median & Mode
concepts.tagline: Beyond the mean: how to find the value at a given probability, where the density peaks, and why skew separates the three centers.

sections.body: The mean is one summary of a distribution, but the exam also asks for the **median** (the 50th percentile), the **mode** (the most likely value), and arbitrary **percentiles** ('the value-at-risk such that only 5% exceeds it'). Each answers a different question, and in a skewed distribution they pull apart in a predictable order you can exploit.

sections.title: Three different notions of 'center'
sections.body: The **median** splits the area under the density in half, half the probability lies on each side. The **mode** is where the density is tallest, the most likely neighborhood. The **mean** is the balance point, the center of mass. For a symmetric distribution all three coincide. Skew the distribution and they spread out: a long right tail drags the mean above the median, which sits above the mode. Percentiles are the language of risk. Actuaries quote **Value-at-Risk** as a percentile of the loss, 'the 99th-percentile loss is the amount exceeded only 1% of the time', and spread is often summarized by the **interquartile range** IQR $=Q_3-Q_1$, the width of the middle 50%. Both are just the percentile machinery $F(\pi_p)=p$ read at chosen $p$ values.

sections.title: Finding each one
sections.body: **$p$-th percentile** $\pi_p$: solve $F(\pi_p) = p$. **Median** $m$: solve $F(m) = 0.5$. **Mode**: maximize $f(x)$, for a differentiable density, solve $f'(x)=0$ and check it is a maximum. For the exponential$(\lambda)$, setting $1-e^{-\lambda \pi_p} = p$ gives $\pi_p = -\frac{1}{\lambda}\ln(1-p)$, so the median is $\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$.

sections.title: VaR, IQR, and the normal quantile
sections.body: **Value-at-Risk** at level $p$ is the percentile $\pi_p$ solving $F(\pi_p)=p$ (equivalently $S(\pi_p)=1-p$). **IQR** $=\pi_{0.75}-\pi_{0.25}$ measures spread robustly, unaffected by extreme tails. For a **normal**, percentiles come straight from a $z$-score: $$\pi_p = \mu + z_p\,\sigma,\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,\ z_{0.975}=1.960,\ z_{0.99}=2.326.$$

sections.title: Percentile of an exponential
sections.body: Claim sizes are exponential with mean 500. Find the 90th percentile (the value exceeded only 10% of the time).
steps: So 90% of claims fall below about 1151, a useful 'value-at-risk' style figure.

sections.title: Mean vs median vs mode on a skewed density
sections.body: A variable has density $f(x) = 2(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$ (it slopes down from a peak at the left). Find the mode, median, and mean, and confirm how they line up.
steps: **Mode**, where the density is tallest: $f(x)=2(1-x)$ decreases across $[0,1]$, so its maximum is at the left edge, $x = 0$. Mode $= 0$.
**Median**, splits the area in half. CDF: $F(x)=\int_0^x 2(1-t)\,dt = 2x - x^2$. Set $2m - m^2 = 0.5 \Rightarrow m^2 - 2m + 0.5 = 0 \Rightarrow m = 1 - \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \approx 0.293$.
**Mean**, the balance point: $E[X]=\int_0^1 x\cdot 2(1-x)\,dx = \int_0^1 (2x - 2x^2)\,dx = 1 - \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.333$.
Line them up: mode $0 <$ median $0.293 <$ mean $0.333$. The long right tail pulls the mean highest, exactly the right-skew ordering mode $<$ median $<$ mean. ✓

sections.title: Value-at-Risk of a normal loss
sections.body: Annual losses are Normal with mean $\mu=200$ and standard deviation $\sigma=50$ (in thousands). Find the $95\%$ Value-at-Risk, the loss exceeded only $5\%$ of the time.
steps: The $95\%$ VaR is the $95$th percentile: solve $F(\pi_{0.95})=0.95$, i.e. find the value $1.645$ SDs above the mean.
Read it back: there is only a $5\%$ chance annual losses exceed about $\$282\text{k}$, exactly the capital-planning figure VaR is built to give.

sections.title: Mean > median > mode for right skew
sections.body: For a right-skewed distribution (long upper tail, lognormal, exponential, most loss models), the ordering is **mean $>$ median $>$ mode**. The rare large values inflate the mean most, the median less, and leave the mode (the peak) alone. If a question shows mean far above median, you are looking at right skew, and the mean is *not* a typical value. This single fact answers many qualitative questions instantly.

sections.title: Percentile means the value, not the probability
sections.body: The $p$-th percentile is the **$x$-value** $\pi_p$ such that $F(\pi_p)=p$, not the probability $p$ itself. Students sometimes report 0.90 when asked for the 90th percentile; the answer is the dollar/time amount. Also: for discrete or mixed distributions the percentile may not be unique (a flat stretch of the CDF), and the median is the conventional choice in that interval.

sections.title: Percentiles can be non-unique for discrete or flat-CDF variables
sections.body: When the CDF is flat over an interval (a gap in a continuous support) or jumps (a discrete variable), the equation $F(\pi_p)=p$ may have a whole interval of solutions or none exactly. The convention is to take the smallest $x$ with $F(x)\ge p$. So the 'median' of a discrete variable can land on a value with $F$ jumping past $0.5$, do not expect a clean $F=0.5$ hit.

cards.front: What exactly is the $p$-th percentile, and what's the classic wrong answer?
cards.back: It's the *$x$-value* $\pi_p$ at which the accumulated probability reaches $p$: solve $F(\pi_p)=p$. The classic slip is reporting $p$ itself (e.g. 0.90) when asked for the 90th percentile, the answer is the dollar/time/loss amount $\pi_p$, not the probability.

cards.front: Why do mean, median, and mode coincide when symmetric but separate under skew?
cards.back: Each measures a different 'center': median halves the area, mode is the density's peak, mean is the balance point. Symmetry makes all three land at the axis of symmetry. A long right tail adds rare large values that pull the *balance point* (mean) outward most, the area-splitting median less, and leave the peak (mode) put, giving mode $<$ median $<$ mean for right skew (reversed for left).

cards.front: How does Value-at-Risk relate to a percentile, and how do you get it for a normal?
cards.back: $p$-level VaR is just the $p$-th percentile of the loss: the amount $\pi_p$ with $F(\pi_p)=p$, exceeded with probability $1-p$. For a normal loss, percentiles are $\pi_p=\mu+z_p\sigma$, so the $95\%$ VaR is $\mu+1.645\sigma$ and the $99\%$ VaR is $\mu+2.326\sigma$, a single $z$-score scaled by $\sigma$ and shifted by $\mu$.

cards.front: Why might the percentile equation $F(\pi_p)=p$ have no exact or no unique solution?
cards.back: If the CDF *jumps* (discrete variable) it can skip past the level $p$ with no $x$ hitting it exactly; if the CDF is *flat* over an interval, many $x$ satisfy $F(x)=p$. The standard fix is to define $\pi_p$ as the smallest $x$ with $F(x)\ge p$, which is why a discrete median may sit at a value where $F$ leaps from below to above $0.5$.

questions.q: Losses are exponential with mean 1000. Find the median.
questions.explain: Median $=\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}=1000\ln 2\approx 693$. Note it is below the mean, right skew.

questions.q: $X$ has CDF $F(x)=x^3$ on $(0,1)$. Find the 25th percentile.
questions.explain: Solve $x^3=0.25\Rightarrow x=0.25^{1/3}\approx 0.63$.

questions.q: A distribution is right-skewed. Which ordering holds?
questions.explain: Right skew (long upper tail) drags the mean highest: mean $>$ median $>$ mode.

questions.q: $X$ has density $f(x)=2x$ on $(0,1)$. Find the mode.
questions.explain: $f(x)=2x$ increases on $(0,1)$, so the density is tallest at the right endpoint $x=1$.

questions.q: For a symmetric, unimodal distribution, the median equals:
choices: both the mean and the mode
questions.explain: Symmetry forces all three measures of center to coincide.

questions.q: Losses follow an exponential distribution with mean 500. Calculate the 75th percentile.
questions.explain: Solve $F(\pi) = 1 - e^{-\pi/500} = 0.75$: $e^{-\pi/500} = 0.25 \Rightarrow \pi = -500\ln(0.25) = 693$. The distractor 347 is the median ($500\ln 2$) and 1151 is the 90th percentile, other percentiles of the same distribution.

questions.q: A random variable has density $f(x) = 12x^2(1-x)$ for $0 < x < 1$. Calculate the mode.
questions.explain: Maximize the density: $f'(x) = 12(2x - 3x^2) = 12x(2 - 3x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = \frac23 \approx 0.667$. This is a Beta$(3,2)$, whose mode $\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha+\beta-2} = \frac{2}{3}$ confirms it. The mean of this density is 0.6, a different center.

concepts.title: Gamma, Beta & Lognormal
concepts.tagline: The three advanced continuous families the exam expects you to recognize: waiting-time sums, bounded proportions, and multiplicative growth.

sections.body: Once you are past uniform, exponential, and normal, three more families show up with real frequency, and each has a *story* that tells you when it appears. **Gamma** is the wait for several Poisson events. **Beta** lives on $[0,1]$ and models proportions. **Lognormal** is what you get when effects multiply instead of add. Recognize the story and you have already picked the distribution.

sections.title: Each family's origin story
sections.body: **Gamma$(\alpha,\theta)$**: add $\alpha$ independent exponentials with mean $\theta$ and you get a Gamma, the total time to the $\alpha$-th arrival. Shape $\alpha$ controls how bell-like it becomes. **Beta$(\alpha,\beta)$**: the natural distribution for a random *fraction*, flexible shapes on $[0,1]$, the conjugate prior for a binomial proportion. **Lognormal**: if $\ln X$ is normal, $X$ is lognormal, the limit of many *multiplicative* shocks, so it models asset prices and loss sizes with a long right tail. These three are less exotic than they look, each is a familiar face in disguise. The **exponential** is just Gamma with shape $\alpha=1$. The **chi-square** with $k$ degrees of freedom is Gamma$(k/2,\,2)$, the workhorse of statistics. And a **uniform$(0,1)$** is Beta$(1,1)$. Seeing gamma as 'stacked exponentials' and beta as 'the flexible $[0,1]$ shape' turns a scary trio into one idea each.

sections.title: Moments worth memorizing
sections.body: **Gamma$(\alpha,\theta)$**: mean $\alpha\theta$, variance $\alpha\theta^2$, MGF $(1-\theta t)^{-\alpha}$. **Beta$(\alpha,\beta)$**: mean $\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}$, variance $\frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}$. **Lognormal**: if $\ln X \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, then $E[X] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = e^{2\mu+\sigma^2}\big(e^{\sigma^2}-1\big)$. Probabilities for the lognormal are done by taking logs and using the normal table.

sections.title: Special cases and gamma additivity
sections.body: **Exponential$(\lambda)$** $=$ Gamma$(1,\,1/\lambda)$. **Chi-square$(k)$** $=$ Gamma$(k/2,\,2)$, mean $k$, variance $2k$. **Gamma additivity** (same scale): independent $\text{Gamma}(\alpha_1,\theta)+\text{Gamma}(\alpha_2,\theta)=\text{Gamma}(\alpha_1+\alpha_2,\theta)$, the shapes add, which is why summing $\alpha$ exponentials of mean $\theta$ gives Gamma$(\alpha,\theta)$. **Beta$(1,1)$** is the Uniform$(0,1)$.

sections.title: A lognormal probability
sections.body: Annual losses $X$ are lognormal with $\mu = 7$ and $\sigma = 2$. Find $P(X > 1000)$, given $\Phi(0.05) = 0.520$.
steps: Take logs: $P(X > 1000) = P(\ln X > \ln 1000)$, and $\ln 1000 \approx 6.908$.
So there is about a 52% chance the annual loss exceeds 1000.

sections.title: Gamma as a sum of waits
sections.body: Claims arrive in a Poisson process; the time between successive claims is exponential with mean $\theta = 2$ hours. Find the mean and standard deviation of the waiting time until the **4th** claim, and name the distribution.
steps: The 4th-arrival time is the sum of 4 independent exponential waits, which is exactly Gamma$(\alpha, \theta) = \text{Gamma}(4, 2)$, that is the Gamma's origin story.
Mean straight from the formula: $E[X] = \alpha\theta = 4(2) = 8$ hours.
Variance: $\mathrm{Var}(X) = \alpha\theta^2 = 4(2^2) = 16$, so SD $= 4$ hours.

Cross-check via the sum: each exponential has mean $2$ and variance $\theta^2 = 4$; for independent variables means and variances add, giving mean $4(2)=8$ and variance $4(4)=16$. ✓ Same answer, confirming Gamma is just stacked exponentials.

sections.title: Adding independent gammas (shapes add)
sections.body: Independent waiting times $X\sim\text{Gamma}(3,2)$ and $Y\sim\text{Gamma}(5,2)$ share the scale $\theta=2$. Find the distribution, mean, and variance of $X+Y$.
steps: Same scale $\theta=2$, so gamma additivity applies and the shapes add: $X+Y\sim\text{Gamma}(3+5,\,2)=\text{Gamma}(8,2)$.
Mean: $\alpha\theta = 8(2) = 16$.
Variance: $\alpha\theta^2 = 8(2^2) = 32$.
Cross-check by adding pieces: means $3(2)+5(2)=16$ and (independent) variances $3(4)+5(4)=32$. ✓ The MGFs confirm it: $(1-2t)^{-3}(1-2t)^{-5}=(1-2t)^{-8}$.

sections.title: Take logs first for anything lognormal
sections.body: Every lognormal *probability* question reduces to a normal one: turn $X$ into $\ln X$, standardize, hit the $Z$-table. Never integrate the lognormal density. And for the Gamma, remember it is just a sum of exponentials, if you see 'time until the 3rd claim' with exponential interarrivals, that total is Gamma$(3,\theta)$ and you can quote mean $3\theta$ and variance $3\theta^2$ without setup.

sections.title: Lognormal mean is not $e^{\mu}$
sections.body: The most punished lognormal error: $E[X] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$, **not** $e^{\mu}$. The quantity $e^{\mu}$ is the *median* of the lognormal; the mean is larger because of the right skew. Forgetting the $+\sigma^2/2$ understates the mean every time. Separately, for the Gamma, $\theta$ is the **scale** (so variance carries $\theta^2$); some texts use rate $\beta = 1/\theta$, check which convention a problem uses.

sections.title: Gamma additivity needs a *common* scale
sections.body: Shapes add only when the gammas share the **same scale $\theta$** (equivalently the same rate). $\text{Gamma}(\alpha_1,\theta)+\text{Gamma}(\alpha_2,\theta)=\text{Gamma}(\alpha_1+\alpha_2,\theta)$, but if the scales differ the sum is *not* a gamma at all. Watch the convention too: scale $\theta$ vs rate $\beta=1/\theta$, the MGF is $(1-\theta t)^{-\alpha}$ in scale form, $(1-t/\beta)^{-\alpha}$ in rate form.

cards.front: How does each family's *story* tell you to pick it on sight?
cards.back: Gamma is the *sum of $\alpha$ exponential waits*, use it for 'time until the $\alpha$-th event' (mean $\alpha\theta$, variance $\alpha\theta^2$). Beta lives on $[0,1]$, use it for a random *proportion or fraction*. Lognormal is what you get when many effects *multiply* (so $\ln X$ is normal), use it for asset prices and loss sizes with a long right tail. Match the mechanism, then quote the moments.

cards.front: Why is the lognormal mean $e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$ rather than $e^\mu$, and how do you get its probabilities?
cards.back: $e^\mu$ is the *median* (the point where $\ln X = \mu$); the right skew drags the mean above it by the factor $e^{\sigma^2/2}$, so $E[X]=e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$, dropping that term understates the mean every time. For any lognormal *probability*, don't integrate the density: take logs to convert to $\ln X \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, standardize, and read the normal table.

cards.front: Why do the shapes add when you sum independent gammas of equal scale?
cards.back: Each Gamma$(\alpha_i,\theta)$ has MGF $(1-\theta t)^{-\alpha_i}$; independence multiplies MGFs, giving $(1-\theta t)^{-(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)}$, which is Gamma$(\alpha_1+\alpha_2,\theta)$ by uniqueness. Intuitively, a Gamma is a stack of exponential waits, so concatenating two stacks (same per-wait scale) just lengthens the stack. Different scales break the common factor and the sum is no longer gamma.

cards.front: Which everyday distributions are special cases of Gamma and Beta?
cards.back: Exponential$(\lambda)=$ Gamma$(1,1/\lambda)$ (shape $1$); Chi-square$(k)=$ Gamma$(k/2,2)$ (mean $k$, variance $2k$); Uniform$(0,1)=$ Beta$(1,1)$. Recognizing these lets you reuse gamma/beta moment formulas instead of re-deriving, e.g. a chi-square's mean and variance fall straight out of $\alpha\theta$ and $\alpha\theta^2$.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Gamma}(3, 4)$ (shape 3, scale 4). Find its mean and variance.
questions.explain: Mean $\alpha\theta=3\cdot4=12$; variance $\alpha\theta^2=3\cdot16=48$.

questions.q: $\ln X \sim N(0, 1)$. Find $E[X]$.
questions.explain: $E[X]=e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}=e^{0+1/2}=\sqrt{e}\approx1.649$, not $e^0=1$, which is the median.

questions.q: $X\sim\text{Beta}(2, 3)$. Find $E[X]$.
questions.explain: Mean $=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}=\frac{2}{2+3}=\frac25$.

questions.q: Interarrival times are exponential with mean 2. The time until the 4th arrival has which distribution?
questions.explain: Sum of 4 independent Exponential(mean 2) is Gamma with shape 4, scale 2.

questions.q: For a lognormal with $\ln X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, the median equals:
questions.explain: The median is $e^{\mu}$ (since the median of $\ln X$ is $\mu$); the mean is the larger $e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$.

questions.q: Annual losses are lognormal with parameters $\mu = 8$ and $\sigma = 1$ (so $\ln X \sim N(8,1)$). Calculate $P(X > e^9)$. (Use $\Phi(1) = 0.841$.)
questions.explain: Take logs: $P(X > e^9) = P(\ln X > 9) = P\!\left(Z > \frac{9-8}{1}\right) = P(Z > 1) = 1 - 0.841 = 0.159$. Reporting 0.841 forgets to take the upper tail.

questions.q: If $\ln X \sim N(4, 2)$ (mean 4, variance 2), calculate $E[X]$.
questions.explain: The lognormal mean is $E[X] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2} = e^{4 + 2/2} = e^{5} \approx 148.4$. The trap answer $e^4 \approx 54.6$ is the median; dropping the $+\sigma^2/2$ understates the mean every time.

modules.title: Multivariate Random Variables
modules.blurb: Two or more variables at once: joint and marginal distributions, covariance and correlation, conditional expectation, sums of random variables, and the Central Limit Theorem that ties the whole exam together.

concepts.title: Joint & Marginal Distributions
concepts.tagline: Two variables share one probability surface. Marginalizing is just summing or integrating out the variable you stopped caring about.

sections.body: When two random variables interact, a loss and its deductible, a claim count and its severity, they share **one joint distribution**, a surface of probability over a plane. Reading that surface (and collapsing it back to one variable) is the core skill of the final module.

sections.title: Marginalize = sum out what you ignore
sections.body: The **joint** $f(x,y)$ is the full surface. To get the **marginal** of $X$ alone, you collapse the surface along the $Y$ direction, sum (discrete) or integrate (continuous) over all $y$. You are pooling together every way $X = x$ could happen, regardless of $Y$. The word *marginal* is literal: old textbooks wrote these sums in the margins.

sections.title: Marginals, independence, and joint expectation
sections.body: Marginal: $f_X(x) = \int f(x,y)\,dy$ (or $\sum_y$). Independence holds iff the joint factors: $f(x,y) = f_X(x)\,f_Y(y)$ for all $x,y$. Expectation of a function: $$E[g(X,Y)] = \iint g(x,y)\,f(x,y)\,dx\,dy$$

sections.title: Marginal from a joint density
sections.body: Let $f(x,y) = x + y$ on the unit square $0 \le x,y \le 1$. Find the marginal $f_X(x)$.
steps: Integrate out $y$ over $[0,1]$: $f_X(x) = \int_0^1 (x + y)\,dy$.
Valid for $0 \le x \le 1$.

sections.title: Marginal over a triangular support
sections.body: Let $f(x,y) = 8xy$ on the triangle $0 < x < y < 1$ (and 0 elsewhere). Find the marginal $f_X(x)$, the support is the part that trips people up.
steps: Fix $x$ and ask which $y$ are allowed: the constraint $x < y < 1$ means $y$ runs from $x$ up to $1$, **not** from $0$ to $1$. Sketching the triangle makes this obvious.
Integrate out $y$ over those correct limits: $f_X(x) = \int_x^1 8xy\,dy = 8x\cdot\dfrac{y^2}{2}\Big|_x^1 = 4x(1 - x^2) = 4x - 4x^3$, for $0 < x < 1$.
Cross-check it is a valid density: $\int_0^1 (4x - 4x^3)\,dx = 2x^2 - x^4\big|_0^1 = 2 - 1 = 1$. ✓
Note independence fails here: the support is a triangle, so knowing $X = x$ restricts $Y$ to $(x,1)$, the variables are dependent no matter how the density looks.

sections.title: Test independence by trying to factor
sections.body: To check independence fast, see whether $f(x,y)$ splits into a pure-$x$ piece times a pure-$y$ piece **over a rectangular region**. If the support is a triangle, or the density tangles $x$ and $y$ together (like $x + y$), they are dependent, no need to compute marginals first.

sections.title: Ignoring the region of support
sections.body: The limits of integration come from the **support**, not always $0$ to $1$. If $X$ and $Y$ live on a triangle like $0 < x < y < 1$, the marginal of $X$ integrates $y$ from $x$ to $1$, not $0$ to $1$. Getting the bounds wrong silently corrupts every downstream answer, sketch the region first.

cards.front: Why does marginalizing mean integrating (or summing) out the other variable?
cards.back: The joint $f(x,y)$ is a probability surface over the plane. The marginal $f_X(x)$ pools *every* way $X=x$ can occur regardless of $Y$, so you collapse the surface along the $Y$ direction, $\int f(x,y)\,dy$ (continuous) or $\sum_y f(x,y)$ (discrete). You're adding up all the $Y$-possibilities to leave a one-variable distribution.

cards.front: Why do the support region and the factoring test decide independence and the integration limits together?
cards.back: The limits come from the *support*: on a triangle like $0<x<y<1$, $y$ runs from $x$ to $1$, not $0$ to $1$, wrong bounds corrupt everything downstream. That same support also signals dependence: independence requires $f(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y)$ over a *rectangular* region, so a triangular support or an $x$-and-$y$-tangled density (like $x+y$) means the variables are dependent, no marginals needed to see it.

questions.q: For $f(x,y) = x+y$ on the unit square, find $E[X]$.
$X$ and $Y$ have joint pmf with $P(0,0)=0.1, P(0,1)=0.2, P(1,0)=0.3, P(1,1)=0.4$. Find the marginal $P(X=1)$.
A joint density is $f(x,y) = 4xy$ on the unit square. Are $X$ and $Y$ independent?
choices: No, the support is a triangle
questions.explain: Over the rectangular unit square, $4xy = (2x)(2y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$, so $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

questions.q: For $f(x,y) = 2$ on $0 < x < y < 1$, find the marginal $f_Y(y)$.
questions.explain: Integrate $x$ from 0 to $y$: $f_Y(y) = \int_0^y 2\,dx = 2y$ for $0<y<1$.

questions.q: The joint density is $f(x,y) = x + y$ on the unit square $0 \le x,y \le 1$. Calculate $P(X < 0.5,\ Y < 0.5)$.
questions.explain: Integrate over the corner: $\int_0^{0.5}\!\int_0^{0.5} (x+y)\,dx\,dy = \int_0^{0.5}\left(0.125 + 0.5y\right)dy = 0.0625 + 0.0625 = 0.125$. Multiplying the marginals as if independent (0.25 × 0.25 region) misses that $x$ and $y$ are tangled.

questions.q: $X$ and $Y$ have joint density $f(x,y) = 4xy$ on the unit square. Calculate $P(X + Y < 1)$.
questions.explain: Integrate over the triangle $x,y>0,\ x+y<1$: $\int_0^1\!\int_0^{1-x} 4xy\,dy\,dx = \int_0^1 2x(1-x)^2\,dx = 1 - \tfrac43 + \tfrac12 = \tfrac16 \approx 0.167$. The trap is integrating over the full square (which gives 1) instead of the constrained region.

concepts.title: Covariance & Correlation
concepts.tagline: How two variables move together, and the formula for the variance of a sum that the exam asks for relentlessly.

sections.body: Covariance measures whether two variables rise and fall together. Its single most-tested consequence: the **variance of a sum** picks up a covariance term. Forget that term and you will systematically miss portfolio and aggregate-loss questions worth real points.

sections.title: Do they move together or against?
sections.body: Positive covariance: when $X$ is above its mean, $Y$ tends to be too, they move *together*. Negative: they move *oppositely*. Zero: no linear relationship. Correlation is just covariance rescaled to $[-1, 1]$ so you can compare across different units, it strips out the magnitudes and keeps only the direction and tightness of the linear link.

sections.title: Covariance, correlation, variance of a sum
sections.body: $$\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]$$ $$\rho = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y}, \quad -1 \le \rho \le 1$$ The headline result: $$\mathrm{Var}(X + Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y) + 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$$

sections.title: Variance of a sum with covariance
sections.body: $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 4$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = 9$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = 2$. Find $\mathrm{Var}(X + Y)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X - Y)$.
steps: For a difference the covariance term flips sign: $\mathrm{Var}(X-Y) = 4 + 9 - 2(2) = 9$.
Note both exceed neither variance alone, covariance shifts them apart.

sections.title: From correlation to a weighted-portfolio variance
sections.body: Two risks have $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 4$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = 9$, and correlation $\rho = 0.5$. A portfolio holds $2X + 3Y$. Find $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$ and then $\mathrm{Var}(2X + 3Y)$.
steps: Recover covariance from correlation by un-rescaling: $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = \rho\,\sigma_X\sigma_Y = 0.5\,(\sqrt{4})(\sqrt{9}) = 0.5(2)(3) = 3$.

Use the general linear-combination rule: $\mathrm{Var}(aX+bY) = a^2\mathrm{Var}(X) + b^2\mathrm{Var}(Y) + 2ab\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$, the scalars enter *squared* on the variances and as $2ab$ on the covariance.

Cross-check the covariance contribution's sign: both weights are positive, so the $+36$ correctly *inflates* the variance, positively correlated risks held in the same direction compound, they don't diversify. ✓

sections.title: Independent → covariance is 0 → variances just add
sections.body: If the problem says independent (or uncorrelated), $\mathrm{Cov} = 0$, so $\mathrm{Var}(X \pm Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y)$, note it is a **plus** even for a difference, because the covariance term that would carry the sign is zero. That subtlety trips up a lot of students.

sections.title: Zero correlation does not mean independent
sections.body: $\rho = 0$ rules out a *linear* relationship, but variables can be strongly dependent in a nonlinear way and still have zero covariance (e.g. $Y = X^2$ with $X$ symmetric about 0). Independence implies zero covariance; the reverse is false. Do not upgrade *uncorrelated* to *independent*.

cards.front: Why does $\mathrm{Var}(X\pm Y)$ carry a $\pm 2\,\mathrm{Cov}$ term, and why does it vanish under independence?
cards.back: Expanding $\mathrm{Var}(X\pm Y)=E[((X\pm Y)-\mu)^2]$ produces the two own-variances plus a cross-term $\pm 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$ that captures how the two move together. If they're independent (or just uncorrelated) that covariance is $0$, so the variances simply add, and crucially it's a *plus* even for $X-Y$, because the sign-carrying term is gone.

cards.front: Why doesn't $\rho = 0$ imply independence?
cards.back: Correlation only detects a *linear* relationship. A variable can depend strongly on another through a nonlinear shape, e.g. $Y=X^2$ with $X$ symmetric about 0 has $\mathrm{Cov}=0$ yet $Y$ is completely determined by $X$. Independence forces $\rho=0$, but the converse fails, never upgrade 'uncorrelated' to 'independent'.

questions.q: $E[XY] = 10$, $E[X] = 3$, $E[Y] = 2$. Find $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$.
$\mathrm{Var}(X)=5$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=8$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=-2$. Find $\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)$.
Two uncorrelated risks each have variance 16. What is the standard deviation of their total?
questions.explain: Uncorrelated: $\mathrm{Var}(X+Y) = 16+16 = 32$, SD $= \sqrt{32} \approx 5.66$.

questions.q: $X$ and $Y$ have $\sigma_X = 2$, $\sigma_Y = 5$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = 4$. Find the correlation $\rho$.
A portfolio is $W = 2X + 3Y$ with $\mathrm{Var}(X)=1$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=2$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0.5$. Find $\mathrm{Var}(W)$.
Random variables satisfy $E[X]=2$, $E[Y]=3$, $E[XY]=8$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=4$, and $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=9$. Calculate the correlation coefficient $\rho_{X,Y}$.
questions.explain: Covariance first: $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] = 8 - 6 = 2$. Then $\rho = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{4}\sqrt{9}} = \frac{2}{6} = 0.333$. Answer 2.0 is the covariance left un-rescaled.

questions.q: $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 5$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = 8$, and $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = -2$. Calculate $\mathrm{Var}(2X - 3Y)$.
questions.explain: $\mathrm{Var}(2X-3Y) = 2^2(5) + (-3)^2(8) + 2(2)(-3)\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) = 20 + 72 + (-12)(-2) = 20 + 72 + 24 = 116$. Dropping the covariance term gives 92; mishandling its sign gives 68.

concepts.title: Conditional Distributions
concepts.tagline: Once you learn $Y=y$, the distribution of $X$ updates. Slice the joint surface, renormalize, and you have the conditional density.

sections.body: Information changes probability. The instant you learn that a policyholder filed exactly two claims, the distribution of their *total loss* shifts. The machinery for that update, slicing the joint distribution and rescaling it, is the **conditional distribution**, and it underpins every credibility, mixture, and double-expectation question on the exam.

sections.title: A conditional density is a renormalized slice
sections.body: Picture the joint surface $f(x,y)$. Fixing $Y = y$ takes a single vertical slice through it. That slice has the right *shape* for the distribution of $X$ given $Y=y$, but its area is only $f_Y(y)$, not 1. Divide by $f_Y(y)$ to rescale the slice back to a legitimate density. That is all a conditional density is: a slice, renormalized so it integrates to 1.

sections.title: Conditional density and expectation
sections.body: $$f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y) = \frac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}$$ The conditional expectation is the mean of that slice: $$E[X \mid Y=y] = \int x\,f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,dx$$ If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, conditioning changes nothing: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y) = f_X(x)$.

sections.title: Conditional density from a joint
sections.body: Let $f(x,y) = 2$ on the triangle $0 < x < y < 1$. Find $f_{X\mid Y}(x \mid y)$ and $E[X \mid Y = y]$.
steps: Marginal of $Y$: $f_Y(y) = \int_0^y 2\,dx = 2y$ for $0 < y < 1$.
Conditional: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y) = \frac{2}{2y} = \frac{1}{y}$ for $0 < x < y$, i.e. $X \mid Y=y$ is Uniform$(0,y)$.
So $E[X \mid Y=y] = \frac{y}{2}$ (mean of a uniform on $(0,y)$).
The conditional turned a 2-D triangle into a simple 1-D uniform once $y$ is fixed.

sections.title: A non-uniform conditional slice
sections.body: Let $f(x,y) = x + y$ on the unit square $0 \le x,y \le 1$. Find the conditional density $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)$ and the conditional mean $E[X\mid Y=y]$.
steps: Divide by the marginal of the variable you condition on: first $f_Y(y) = \int_0^1 (x+y)\,dx = \tfrac12 + y$.
Conditional density: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y) = \dfrac{x+y}{y + \tfrac12}$ for $0 \le x \le 1$, a *tilted* density, not uniform, because the slice is not flat.

Conditional mean: $E[X\mid Y=y] = \displaystyle\int_0^1 x\cdot\frac{x+y}{y+\tfrac12}\,dx = \frac{\int_0^1 (x^2 + xy)\,dx}{y+\tfrac12} = \frac{\tfrac13 + \tfrac{y}{2}}{y+\tfrac12} = \frac{3y+2}{6y+3}$.

Cross-check at $y=0$: the slice becomes $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid 0) = 2x$, whose mean is $\tfrac23$; the formula gives $\tfrac{2}{3}$ too. ✓ And note $E[X\mid Y=y]$ genuinely depends on $y$, confirming $X$ and $Y$ are dependent.

sections.title: Recognize the slice as a named distribution
sections.body: After you divide by the marginal, the conditional density is often a *standard* distribution in disguise, uniform, exponential, beta. The moment you recognize it (as Uniform$(0,y)$ above), you can quote its mean and variance instead of integrating. This shortcut is enormous in double-expectation problems, where you need $E[X\mid Y]$ as a function of $Y$.

sections.title: Divide by the right marginal, and keep the support
sections.body: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)$ divides by $f_Y(y)$, the marginal of the variable you *conditioned on*, not the one you want. Swapping them is a classic error. And the conditional's support depends on $y$: above, $X$ ranges only over $(0,y)$, not $(0,1)$. Carrying the wrong support breaks the normalization and every expectation after it.

cards.front: Why is the conditional density a *slice divided by the marginal*, and which marginal?
cards.back: Fixing $Y=y$ takes a vertical slice $f(x,y)$ through the joint surface; that slice has the right *shape* for $X\mid Y=y$ but its area is only $f_Y(y)$, not 1. Dividing by $f_Y(y)$, the marginal of the variable you *conditioned on*, not the one you want, rescales it to a legitimate density. Its support also shrinks with $y$ (e.g. $X$ only on $(0,y)$), and you must carry that.

cards.front: Why does recognizing the slice as a named distribution (or independence) save so much work?
cards.back: After dividing out the marginal, the conditional is often a standard form in disguise, Uniform$(0,y)$, exponential, beta, so you can quote its mean/variance instead of integrating, which is gold in double-expectation problems that need $E[X\mid Y]$ as a function of $Y$. And if $X,Y$ are independent, conditioning changes nothing: $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=f_X(x)$.

questions.q: $f(x,y)=2$ on $0<x<y<1$. Find $E[X\mid Y=0.6]$.
If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)$ equals:
questions.explain: Independence means conditioning adds no information: the conditional is just the marginal $f_X(x)$.

questions.q: Joint pmf: $P(X{=}1,Y{=}1)=0.2$, and the marginal $P(Y{=}1)=0.5$. Find $P(X{=}1\mid Y{=}1)$.
$X\mid Y=y$ is exponential with mean $y$. Find $E[X\mid Y=4]$.
questions.explain: An exponential with mean $y$ has $E[X\mid Y=y]=y$, so $E[X\mid Y=4]=4$.

questions.q: $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}$ for $0<x<y<1$ describes $X\mid Y=y$ as:
questions.explain: Constant density $1/y$ on $(0,y)$ is the Uniform$(0,y)$ distribution.

questions.q: The joint density is $f(x,y) = 2$ on the triangle $0 < x < y < 1$. Calculate $E[Y \mid X = 0.4]$.
questions.explain: Marginal $f_X(x) = \int_x^1 2\,dy = 2(1-x)$, so $f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x) = \frac{2}{2(1-x)} = \frac{1}{1-x}$ on $(x,1)$, i.e. $Y\mid X=x$ is Uniform$(x,1)$. Thus $E[Y\mid X=0.4] = \frac{0.4+1}{2} = 0.7$. Forgetting the support starts at $x$ (using Uniform$(0,1)$) gives 0.5.

questions.q: A joint pmf is $P(1,1)=0.1$, $P(1,2)=0.2$, $P(2,1)=0.3$, $P(2,2)=0.4$ (first coordinate $X$, second $Y$). Calculate $E[Y \mid X = 2]$.
questions.explain: $P(X=2) = 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7$, so $P(Y=1\mid X=2) = \frac{0.3}{0.7}=\frac37$ and $P(Y=2\mid X=2) = \frac47$. Then $E[Y\mid X=2] = 1\cdot\frac37 + 2\cdot\frac47 = \frac{11}{7} \approx 1.571$. Using the unconditional split (ignoring the renormalization by $P(X=2)$) gives the wrong weights.

concepts.title: Double Expectation & the Variance Decomposition
concepts.tagline: $E[X]=E[E[X\mid Y]]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)]+\mathrm{Var}(E[X\mid Y])$, the two laws that crack every mixture problem.

sections.body: Some of the highest-value questions on Exam P look impossible head-on: a Poisson number of claims, each of random size; a loss whose mean depends on an unknown risk class. The key that unlocks all of them is **conditioning**, solve the easy problem given the hidden variable, then average over it. Two laws make this airtight: the **law of total expectation** and the **law of total variance**.

sections.title: Average the conditional answers
sections.body: If you knew the risk class $Y$, finding $E[X\mid Y]$ would be easy. You do not know $Y$, so treat $E[X\mid Y]$ as a *random variable* (it depends on which $Y$ you land in) and average it: $E[X]=E[E[X\mid Y]]$. Variance splits the same way but into **two** pieces: the average spread *within* each class, plus the spread *between* the class means. Total uncertainty = uncertainty inside groups + uncertainty across groups.

sections.title: The two laws
sections.body: **Total expectation:** $$E[X] = E\big[E[X\mid Y]\big]$$ **Total variance:** $$\mathrm{Var}(X) = \underbrace{E\big[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)\big]}_{\text{within (expected process var)}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}\big(E[X\mid Y]\big)}_{\text{between (variance of hypothetical means)}}$$ In credibility language these are the *expected process variance* and the *variance of the hypothetical means*.

widget.caption: Two risk classes, each with its own mean and spread. Watch how the **total** variance is always the within-class variance plus the between-class variance, and how widening the gap between the class means inflates the 'between' term while leaving the 'within' term untouched.

sections.title: A two-class mixture
sections.body: 70% of drivers are low-risk with mean claim 1 and variance 1; 30% are high-risk with mean claim 4 and variance 9. Find $E[X]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ for a randomly chosen driver.

sections.title: A compound Poisson aggregate loss
sections.body: The number of claims is $N \sim \text{Poisson}(3)$, and each claim has mean $100$ and variance $400$, independent of $N$ and of each other. Find $E[S]$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S)$ for the aggregate $S = X_1 + \dots + X_N$.
steps: Mean by the law of total expectation: $E[S] = E[N]\,E[X] = 3(100) = 300$.
Variance by the law of total variance (within + between): $\mathrm{Var}(S) = E[N]\,\mathrm{Var}(X) + (E[X])^2\,\mathrm{Var}(N)$. Here $\mathrm{Var}(N) = 3$ (Poisson mean = variance).
Cross-check with the Poisson shortcut $\mathrm{Var}(S) = \lambda\,E[X^2]$, where $E[X^2] = \mathrm{Var}(X) + (E[X])^2 = 400 + 10000 = 10400$: $3(10400) = 31200$. ✓ Both routes agree.

sections.title: Compound sums: $E[S]=E[N]E[X]$
sections.body: For a compound sum $S = X_1 + \dots + X_N$ where $N$ is random and the $X_i$ are iid (mean $\mu$, variance $\sigma^2$), the laws give two memorizable results: $E[S] = E[N]\,\mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(S) = E[N]\,\sigma^2 + \mu^2\,\mathrm{Var}(N)$. If $N$ is Poisson$(\lambda)$ (so mean = variance = $\lambda$), this collapses to the elegant $\mathrm{Var}(S) = \lambda\,E[X^2]$. Memorize these, they appear every sitting.

sections.title: Don't drop the between-group term
sections.body: The most expensive error in this topic: computing only $E[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)]$ and calling it the variance. That ignores the variance *between* the conditional means and **understates** total variance. Total variance is always the sum of both pieces. Symmetric warning: $E[X]$ uses only the first law, but $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ needs both, never reuse the expectation shortcut for variance.

cards.front: Why does $E[X]=E[E[X\mid Y]]$ work, what's the strategy it encodes?
cards.back: When a hidden variable $Y$ (risk class, claim count) makes $X$ easy *once known*, compute the easy conditional answer $E[X\mid Y]$, then treat it as a random variable, it depends on which $Y$ you land in, and average over $Y$. Solve given the unknown, then average out the unknown. That two-step is the whole engine behind mixture and compound problems.

cards.front: Why does $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ split into two terms, and what breaks if you drop one?
cards.back: Total uncertainty is the spread *within* each class plus the spread *between* the class means: $\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)]+\mathrm{Var}(E[X\mid Y])$. Keeping only the within-term ($E[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)]$) ignores how much the class means differ and *understates* the variance. Widening the gap between class means inflates the between-term while leaving the within-term untouched, so both are essential.

questions.q: $E[X\mid Y]=2Y$ and $E[Y]=5$. Find $E[X]$.
Number of claims $N\sim$ Poisson$(3)$; each claim has mean 100, variance 400. Find $E[S]$ for the aggregate $S$.
Same setup: $N\sim$ Poisson$(3)$, claim mean 100, variance 400. Find $\mathrm{Var}(S)$.
questions.explain: Poisson: $\mathrm{Var}(S)=\lambda E[X^2]=\lambda(\sigma^2+\mu^2)=3(400+10000)=3(10400)=31200$.

questions.q: A mixture: with prob 0.5, $X\mid Y$ has mean 2; with prob 0.5, mean 6. Each conditional has variance 0. Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$.
Which quantity does $E[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)]$ alone fail to capture?
choices: The variance between the group means
Nothing, it is the full variance
questions.explain: It is only the within-group piece; total variance also needs $\mathrm{Var}(E[X\mid Y])$, the between-group spread.

questions.q: The number of injuries $N$ on a given day is Poisson with mean $\Lambda$, where $\Lambda$ itself is uniformly distributed on $[0, 4]$. Calculate $\mathrm{Var}(N)$.
questions.explain: Law of total variance: $\mathrm{Var}(N) = E[\mathrm{Var}(N\mid\Lambda)] + \mathrm{Var}(E[N\mid\Lambda]) = E[\Lambda] + \mathrm{Var}(\Lambda) = 2 + \frac{4^2}{12} = 2 + 1.333 = 3.333$. Answer 2.0 keeps only $E[\Lambda]$ (treating $\Lambda$ as fixed); 1.333 keeps only $\mathrm{Var}(\Lambda)$.

questions.q: The number of claims $N \sim$ Poisson$(4)$, and each claim has mean 200 and variance 100, independent of $N$. Calculate $\mathrm{Var}(S)$ for the aggregate $S = X_1 + \dots + X_N$.
questions.explain: For a compound Poisson, $\mathrm{Var}(S) = \lambda\,E[X^2] = \lambda(\mathrm{Var}(X) + E[X]^2) = 4(100 + 200^2) = 4(40100) = 160400$. Keeping only $\lambda\,\mathrm{Var}(X) = 400$ omits the severity-mean contribution; $\lambda\,E[X]^2 = 160000$ omits the process variance.

concepts.title: Sums of Random Variables & Convolutions
concepts.tagline: The density of $X+Y$ is a convolution. But for the named families, sums stay in the family, and that shortcut is the exam answer.

sections.body: Add two independent random variables and the distribution of the total is a **convolution**, a sliding integral that blends the two densities. The exam almost never wants you to grind out that integral. Instead it rewards knowing which families are *closed under addition*: add two of the same kind and you get the same kind, with parameters that simply combine.

sections.title: Every split that lands on the target
sections.body: To find $P(X+Y = s)$, you sum over every way the total can be $s$: $X=k$ and $Y=s-k$, for all $k$. That sum-over-splits *is* the convolution. Geometrically you slide one density across the other and integrate the overlap. Most of the time, though, the algebra collapses because the MGFs multiply into a recognizable form, so you skip the integral entirely.

sections.title: Convolution and the family-closure rules
sections.body: Discrete: $P(X+Y=s)=\sum_k P(X=k)P(Y=s-k)$. Continuous: $f_{X+Y}(s)=\int f_X(x)f_Y(s-x)\,dx$. **Closure shortcuts (independent):** Normal $+$ Normal $=$ Normal (means and variances add). Poisson$(\lambda)+$Poisson$(\mu)=$Poisson$(\lambda+\mu)$. Binomial$(m,p)+$Binomial$(n,p)=$Binomial$(m+n,p)$. Gamma$(\alpha_1,\theta)+$Gamma$(\alpha_2,\theta)=$Gamma$(\alpha_1+\alpha_2,\theta)$, same scale required.

sections.title: Sum of independent normals
sections.body: $X\sim N(3,4)$ and $Y\sim N(1,9)$ are independent. Find the distribution of $X+Y$ and $P(X+Y > 7)$ given $\Phi(0.5)=0.691$.
steps: Normals are closed under addition: $X+Y \sim N(3+1,\ 4+9) = N(4, 13)$, means add, variances add.
Standardize using the SD $\sqrt{13} \approx 3.606$ (the SD, not the variance): $Z = \dfrac{7-4}{\sqrt{13}} \approx 0.832$.
The whole problem reduced to one normal because the family is closed, no convolution integral.

sections.title: A convolution by hand, and why closure matches it
sections.body: $X \sim \text{Poisson}(1)$ and $Y \sim \text{Poisson}(2)$ are independent. Compute $P(X+Y = 1)$ directly from the convolution, then confirm it with the closure shortcut.
steps: Convolution sums over every split that lands on the target $s=1$: $P(X+Y=1) = P(X=0)P(Y=1) + P(X=1)P(Y=0)$.
Closure shortcut: independent Poissons add, so $X+Y \sim \text{Poisson}(1+2) = \text{Poisson}(3)$, giving $P(X+Y=1) = \dfrac{e^{-3}3^1}{1!} = 3e^{-3}$.
Both give $3e^{-3} \approx 0.149$. ✓ The convolution *is* the closure rule, the shortcut just skips the sum-over-splits.

sections.title: Use MGFs to prove closure instantly
sections.body: Closure is just MGF multiplication. Poisson MGF is $e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}$; multiply two and the exponents add to $(\lambda+\mu)$, Poisson again. Gamma MGF is $(1-\theta t)^{-\alpha}$; multiply and the shapes add (but only if $\theta$ matches). If you ever forget a closure rule, multiply the MGFs and read off the result, faster and safer than recalling the convolution.

sections.title: Closure needs matching parameters and independence
sections.body: Binomials add only with the **same $p$**; Gammas add only with the **same scale $\theta$**. Mismatched parameters break closure, the sum is *not* in the family, and you are back to a convolution or CLT approximation. And every closure rule assumes **independence**: dependent sums pick up covariance and the simple parameter-adding fails.

cards.front: Why is the density of an independent sum a convolution?
cards.back: To get $P(X+Y=s)$ you add up *every* way the total can be $s$: $X=k$ paired with $Y=s-k$, over all $k$. That sum-over-splits is $\sum_k P(X=k)P(Y=s-k)$ (discrete) or $\int f_X(x)f_Y(s-x)\,dx$ (continuous), geometrically, sliding one density across the other and integrating the overlap.

cards.front: Why does family closure work, and what two conditions can break it?
cards.back: Independent sums multiply MGFs, and for closed families that product is the same family's MGF with parameters combined, e.g. Poisson exponents add to $\lambda+\mu$, normal means and variances add. It breaks if (1) parameters don't match (Binomials need the same $p$, Gammas the same scale $\theta$) or (2) the variables aren't independent, then covariance enters and simple parameter-adding fails.

questions.q: $X\sim N(2,5)$ and $Y\sim N(3,4)$ independent. The distribution of $X+Y$ is:
questions.explain: Means add: $2+3=5$. Variances add: $5+4=9$. So $N(5,9)$.

questions.q: $X\sim$ Poisson$(2)$, $Y\sim$ Poisson$(5)$, independent. Find $P(X+Y=0)$.
questions.explain: $X+Y\sim$ Poisson$(7)$, so $P(X+Y=0)=e^{-7}$.

questions.q: Sum of 5 independent Exponential(mean 3) variables has which distribution?
questions.explain: Exponentials are Gamma$(1,\theta)$; five with $\theta=3$ sum to Gamma$(5,3)$.

questions.q: $X\sim$ Bin$(4,0.3)$ and $Y\sim$ Bin$(6,0.3)$ independent. Then $X+Y\sim$:
questions.explain: Same $p=0.3$, so the counts add: Bin$(4+6,0.3)=$ Bin$(10,0.3)$.

questions.q: $X\sim$ Bin$(4,0.3)$ and $Y\sim$ Bin$(6,0.5)$ independent. Is $X+Y$ binomial?
questions.explain: Binomial closure needs a common $p$. With $p=0.3$ vs $0.5$, the sum is not binomial.

questions.q: $X \sim N(50, 100)$ and $Y \sim N(30, 44)$ are independent. Calculate $P(X + Y > 92)$. (Use $\Phi(1) = 0.841$.)
questions.explain: Normals are closed under addition: $X+Y \sim N(80, 144)$, SD $= 12$. Standardize: $Z = \frac{92-80}{12} = 1$, so $P(X+Y>92) = 1 - \Phi(1) = 0.159$. Adding the SDs ($10+\sqrt{44}$) instead of the variances is the usual trap.

questions.q: $X \sim$ Poisson$(1.5)$ and $Y \sim$ Poisson$(2.5)$ are independent. Calculate $P(X + Y = 2)$.
questions.explain: Independent Poissons add: $X+Y \sim$ Poisson$(4)$. So $P(X+Y=2) = \frac{e^{-4}4^2}{2!} = 8e^{-4} \approx 0.147$. Using only one rate (e.g. Poisson(1.5) or (2.5)) gives the off-values.

concepts.title: Order Statistics: Min, Max & Range
concepts.tagline: Sort $n$ independent draws and ask about the smallest or largest. The min and max have clean CDF shortcuts the exam tests directly.

sections.body: Insurance lives at the extremes: the *largest* claim drives reinsurance, the *first* failure ends a warranty. These are **order statistics**, what you get when you sort a sample and look at the ends. The minimum and maximum have shortcut formulas so clean you should never integrate a density to find them.

sections.title: Max via 'all below', min via 'all above'
sections.body: The maximum of $n$ draws is $\le y$ exactly when **every** draw is $\le y$, that is one event repeated $n$ times. By independence the probabilities multiply, so the max's CDF is $[F(y)]^n$. The minimum is $> y$ exactly when **all** draws exceed $y$, giving survival $[1-F(y)]^n$. Both reduce a sorting question to raising a single CDF to the $n$-th power.

sections.title: Min and max distributions (iid sample)
sections.body: For $n$ iid draws with CDF $F$: **Maximum** $Y_{(n)}=\max$: $$F_{\max}(y)=[F(y)]^n$$ **Minimum** $Y_{(1)}=\min$: $$P(\min > y)=[1-F(y)]^n,\quad F_{\min}(y)=1-[1-F(y)]^n$$ Differentiate for densities: $f_{\max}(y)=n[F(y)]^{n-1}f(y)$ and $f_{\min}(y)=n[1-F(y)]^{n-1}f(y)$.

sections.title: Minimum of exponentials stays exponential
sections.body: $n=3$ independent components each have lifetime Exponential$(\lambda)$. Find the distribution of the first failure, $\min(X_1,X_2,X_3)$.
steps: Each survival is $P(X_i>y)=e^{-\lambda y}$.
$P(\min > y)=[e^{-\lambda y}]^3 = e^{-3\lambda y}$.
That is the survival function of an Exponential with rate $3\lambda$.
So the first of $n$ iid exponentials is Exponential$(n\lambda)$, the rates add. Its mean is $\frac{1}{3\lambda}$.

sections.title: Maximum of uniforms: CDF, density, and mean
sections.body: $U_1, \dots, U_n$ are iid Uniform$(0,1)$. Find the CDF and density of the maximum $M = \max U_i$, and its mean.
steps: Use 'all below': $M \le y$ means every $U_i \le y$. With $F(y) = y$ on $[0,1]$ and independence, $F_M(y) = [F(y)]^n = y^n$.
Differentiate (chain rule keeps the inner $f(y)=1$): $f_M(y) = n y^{n-1}$ on $[0,1]$, this is a Beta$(n,1)$ density.
Mean: $E[M] = \int_0^1 y\cdot n y^{n-1}\,dy = n\int_0^1 y^n\,dy = \dfrac{n}{n+1}$.

Sanity check: for $n=3$, $E[M] = \tfrac34$, the largest of 3 uniforms sits well above the single-draw mean of $\tfrac12$, and as $n\to\infty$ the max creeps toward 1, exactly as $\frac{n}{n+1}$ predicts. ✓

sections.title: The minimum of exponentials adds the rates
sections.body: A reflex worth owning: $\min$ of independent exponentials with rates $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ is itself exponential with rate $\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_n$. (For equal rates, $n\lambda$.) This is the 'competing risks / first event' shortcut, whenever several exponential clocks race, the winner's time is exponential with the summed rate. No integration, just add rates.

sections.title: Max is not symmetric to min, and don't forget the chain rule
sections.body: The max uses $[F(y)]^n$ (all below); the min uses the *survival* $[1-F(y)]^n$ (all above), they are **not** mirror formulas, and swapping them is a frequent slip. When differentiating to get a density, remember the chain rule pulls down the inner $f(y)$: $f_{\max}(y)=n[F(y)]^{n-1}f(y)$, not just $n[F(y)]^{n-1}$.

cards.front: Why is the max's CDF $[F(y)]^n$ but the min's *survival* $[1-F(y)]^n$, and why aren't they mirror formulas?
cards.back: The max is $\le y$ exactly when *all* $n$ draws are $\le y$, so by independence the probabilities multiply: $F_{\max}(y)=[F(y)]^n$. The min is $>y$ exactly when *all* draws *exceed* $y$, so it's the *survival* that powers up: $P(\min>y)=[1-F(y)]^n$. One works on the CDF, the other on the survival function, swapping them is the classic slip.

cards.front: Why does the minimum of independent exponentials have the summed rate?
cards.back: Each survival is $e^{-\lambda_i y}$, so $P(\min>y)=\prod e^{-\lambda_i y}=e^{-(\sum\lambda_i)y}$, the survival of an exponential with rate $\sum\lambda_i$. Intuitively several exponential 'clocks' race and the first to fire wins; the failure rates add, so the winner's time is exponential with the combined rate (the competing-risks shortcut).

questions.q: $U_1,\dots,U_4$ are iid Uniform$(0,1)$. Find $P(\max \le 0.5)$.
Three iid Exponential(rate 2) lifetimes. The minimum is exponential with rate:
questions.explain: Rates of the minimum add: $2+2+2=6$.

questions.q: $X_1,\dots,X_n$ iid with CDF $F$. The CDF of the minimum is:
Two iid Uniform$(0,1)$ draws. Find $P(\min > 0.3)$.
For $n$ iid Uniform$(0,1)$, the density of the maximum is $f_{\max}(y)=$:
Three independent components have exponential lifetimes with failure rates 1, 2, and 3 per year. Calculate the expected time until the first component fails.
questions.explain: The minimum of independent exponentials is exponential with the summed rate: $1+2+3 = 6$. Its mean is $\frac{1}{6} \approx 0.167$ years. Averaging the three individual means ($\frac{1+0.5+0.333}{3} = 0.611$) is wrong, rates add, not means.

questions.q: Five independent observations are drawn from a Uniform$(0,1)$ distribution. Calculate $P(\max \le 0.8)$.
questions.explain: The max is $\le 0.8$ exactly when all five draws are $\le 0.8$: $[F(0.8)]^5 = (0.8)^5 = 0.328$. The bare 0.8 is a single draw; $1-0.8^5 = 0.672$ is the complement.

concepts.title: Sums & the Central Limit Theorem
concepts.tagline: Add enough independent variables and the bell appears no matter where you started. The theorem that quietly powers the whole exam.

sections.body: The Central Limit Theorem is the closest thing probability has to magic: sum enough independent pieces and the total is approximately **normal**, regardless of the shape you started with. The SOA uses it to turn ugly aggregate-loss questions into a single $Z$-table lookup.

sections.title: Averaging washes out the weirdness
sections.body: Each individual variable might be skewed, lumpy, discrete, anything. But when you add many independent copies, their idiosyncrasies cancel and the sum's distribution smooths into a bell centered at $n\mu$. The more terms, the better the approximation. This is why the normal distribution shows up everywhere: most real quantities are sums of many small independent effects.

sections.title: Mean and variance of a sum, then standardize
sections.body: For independent $X_1,\dots,X_n$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$: $$E\Big[\sum X_i\Big] = n\mu, \quad \mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum X_i\Big] = n\sigma^2$$ The CLT says the sum is approximately $N(n\mu,\, n\sigma^2)$, so $$Z = \frac{\sum X_i - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}$$ is approximately standard normal.

sections.title: Aggregate claims via the CLT
sections.body: 100 independent claims each have mean 500 and SD 200. Approximate $P(\text{total} > 53{,}000)$.
steps: Total mean $= 100 \times 500 = 50{,}000$. Total variance $= 100 \times 200^2 = 4{,}000{,}000$, so total SD $= 2000$.

sections.title: Normal approximation to a binomial, with continuity correction
sections.body: A fair coin is flipped 100 times. Use the CLT to approximate $P(X \ge 60)$, where $X$ is the number of heads.
steps: $X \sim \text{Binomial}(100, 0.5)$ is a sum of 100 iid Bernoullis, so the CLT applies. Mean $= np = 50$; variance $= np(1-p) = 25$, so SD $= 5$.
Apply the **continuity correction**: a discrete '$X \ge 60$' becomes the continuous '$Y > 59.5$', spread each integer's probability over a unit-wide bar and cut at the bar's edge.

Cross-check the correction's effect: skipping it gives $Z = \frac{60-50}{5} = 2.0 \Rightarrow 0.0228$. The half-unit shift matters for a discrete sum, the corrected $0.0287$ is closer to the exact binomial value. ✓

sections.title: SD of a sum grows like √n, not n
sections.body: The *variance* of a sum scales with $n$, so the *standard deviation* scales with $\sqrt{n}$. That is why averages get tighter slowly: to halve the SD of an average you need *four times* the sample. Whenever you standardize a sum, the denominator is $\sigma\sqrt{n}$, never $\sigma n$.

sections.title: Adding standard deviations directly
sections.body: You cannot add standard deviations, only **variances** add (for independent variables). To combine spreads, square to variance, add, then square-root back. Writing $\mathrm{SD}(X+Y) = \mathrm{SD}(X) + \mathrm{SD}(Y)$ is wrong and inflates the spread badly.

widget.caption: Pick the most non-normal source you can, exponential, bimodal, a coin flip, then raise $n$ and watch the histogram of sample means collapse into a bell. That convergence is the entire justification for the $Z$-table shortcut you use on aggregate-loss questions.

cards.front: Why does a sum of many independent variables become normal no matter where you started?
cards.back: Each term may be skewed, lumpy, or discrete, but adding many independent copies lets their individual quirks cancel out, and the total smooths into a bell centered at $n\mu$ with variance $n\sigma^2$. The more terms, the better the fit, which is why most real quantities (sums of many small effects) end up roughly normal, and why an aggregate-loss question collapses to one $Z$-lookup.

cards.front: Why does the SD of a sum scale like $\sqrt{n}$, and why can't you add SDs directly?
cards.back: For independent variables only *variances* add, so $n$ iid terms give variance $n\sigma^2$ and therefore SD $\sigma\sqrt{n}$, not $\sigma n$. To combine two spreads you square to variance, add, then square-root back; writing $\mathrm{SD}(X+Y)=\mathrm{SD}(X)+\mathrm{SD}(Y)$ overstates the spread. (This $\sqrt{n}$ growth is also why halving an average's SD needs $4\times$ the data.)

questions.q: A sum of 64 iid variables each has mean 10 and SD 4. Find the mean and SD of the sum.
questions.explain: Mean $= 64\times10 = 640$. SD $= 4\sqrt{64} = 4\times8 = 32$.

questions.q: The average of 100 iid claims (mean 20, SD 5) is taken. What is the SD of the sample mean?
questions.explain: SD of the mean $= \sigma/\sqrt{n} = 5/\sqrt{100} = 5/10 = 0.5$.

questions.q: Total of 50 independent losses (each mean 100, variance 400). Approximate $P(\text{total} < 4800)$ using $\Phi(-1.414)=0.079$.
Two independent variables have SDs 3 and 4. What is the SD of their sum?
questions.explain: Variances add: $9 + 16 = 25$, so SD $= \sqrt{25} = 5$, not $3+4=7$.

questions.q: To halve the standard deviation of a sample mean, you must multiply the sample size by:
questions.explain: SD of the mean is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. Halving it needs $\sqrt{n}$ to double, i.e. $n$ to quadruple.

questions.q: A portfolio has 200 independent claims, each with mean 30 and standard deviation 10. Using the CLT, calculate the approximate probability the total exceeds 6300. (Use $\Phi(2.12) = 0.983$.)
questions.explain: Total mean $= 200(30) = 6000$; total variance $= 200(10^2) = 20000$, so SD $= 141.4$. Standardize: $Z = \frac{6300-6000}{141.4} = 2.12$, giving $P > 6300 \approx 1 - 0.983 = 0.017$. Using SD $= 200(10)$ or $10$ alone breaks the $\sqrt{n}$ scaling.

questions.q: 100 independent claims each have mean 500 and standard deviation 200. Using the CLT, calculate the approximate probability that the sample mean exceeds 540. (Use $\Phi(2) = 0.977$.)
questions.explain: The sample mean has SD $\sigma/\sqrt{n} = 200/\sqrt{100} = 20$. Standardize: $Z = \frac{540-500}{20} = 2$, so $P(\bar X > 540) \approx 1 - 0.977 = 0.023$. Using $\sigma = 200$ as the SD of the mean (forgetting $\div\sqrt{n}$) gives $Z=0.2$ and the wrong 0.421.
